content.thinking:
I notice the error rate actually improved, so latency is the real impact axis, not errors. I should avoid restating the given figures as if I'd computed them myself or offering my own numbers—the actual cost was measured from what the shop took, not something for me to calculate.

An important caveat: recovery metrics show the service returned to baseline at 18:14, just before the revert was applied at 18:14:36, meaning the mitigation may not have been the actual cause of recovery—worth flagging as an assumption, especially since this same flag revert reportedly failed to help in a prior incident. I'll frame the timeline using the given event window (18:09 to 18:14 UTC) rather than deriving a duration figure myself, and focus the write-up on root cause, executive summary, and assumptions while steering clear of restating any impact numbers.

I'll avoid naming internal components in the executive summary, referring simply to "the online shop's account page" where needed. My assumptions list should cover: the causal link between the flag toggle and recovery being based on time correlation rather than direct measurement; the ambiguity around whether the revert or natural recovery gets credit; the prior failed use of this same flag revert; that impact was tail latency rather than error rate (which stayed flat or improved); the limited observability window (six hours of metrics, nine minutes of logs, no deeper dependency telemetry); and that the draft PR addressing this at the code level was never merged.

assumptions: Causation is inferred from timing alone. The flag reaching full rollout coincides with the latency jump, and nothing else changed in the preceding window, but no profiling or trace evidence tied the new rendering code to the slow requests.

The service is recorded as recovered at 18:14, roughly thirty seconds before the flag was actually reverted at 18:14:36. The mitigation was marked CONFIRMED because the service was at baseline when it was re-checked at 18:15:09; that check cannot distinguish the revert working from the service having already recovered on its own. Treat 'revert fixed it' as unverified.

Reverting this same flag was tried on an earlier incident (e312780c) and the service did not recover, which is why the responder initially deprioritised it. That prior failure is unexplained and weakens the case that this flag is the sole cause.
The latency figures behind the diagnosis come from the investigator's reading of the metrics; the log lines collected contain no latency data, only flag-evaluation counts and error-rate warnings.

The ClientDisconnected errors on the account page appear before, during and after onset at a steady low level and were treated as pre-existing background noise rather than incident signal. They were not investigated further.
Dependencies (io-pricing, io-summary-cache, io-pay) were ruled out on the absence of errors in nine minutes of io-shop's own logs, not on their own telemetry.

Only the service's own logs and a window of production change events were examined; no customer reports or downstream service impact were checked, so affected-user scope is inferred from the affected code path.
input.executive_summary: Between 18:09 and 18:14 UTC on 26 September 2026, the account page of the online shop became slow to load for the customers who hit the worst of it. A new "monthly spend" feature was being switched on for shoppers during those minutes, and the page's slowest responses degraded sharply as it reached everyone. Typical page loads were unaffected, and the share of requests that failed outright did not increase during the incident — the harm was waiting, not errors. The automated responder picked the incident up about a minute after the alert, identified the feature switch as the likely cause, and switched it back off; the shop was measuring normal again by the time that change was verified. A draft code change addressing the underlying slowness has been opened for review and is not yet merged, so the feature remains off pending that work.
input.root_cause: The `monthly-spend-feature` flag was rolled out from off to on across io-shop's account-page rendering path at 18:09-18:10, and p99 latency on that path jumped from roughly 200ms to the 1300-2000ms range at exactly that moment while p50 stayed flat — a tail-latency regression in the new rendering code, not a general slowdown or a dependency failure. No other production change, and no error or slowness in io-pricing, io-summary-cache or io-pay, was recorded in the window, so the flag is the only recorded change that lines up with onset. Note the caveat below: the metrics show the service back at baseline at 18:14, before the flag was reverted at 18:14:36, so the correlation is strong but the revert's contribution to recovery is not established.
